newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks likely to rise further.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks likely to rise further.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are likely to extend gains in the coming week, propelled by more buying by pension funds and other domestic institutional investors after returning from a long weekend on Tuesday, brokers said.
"The recent rise has been so sudden that market participants are beginning to feel afraid of being left behind," said Nobuhiro Kaneda, general manager at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.

On Friday, due to a wave of pension-motored purchases, the 225-share Nikkei average rose 239.42 points or 1.24 percent to end at 19,514.75, jumping above the previous closing high for 1997 of 19,446.00 set on January 6, the first trading day of year.
The last time the benchmark index closed above the 19,500 hurdle was on Christmas Day, when it ended at 19,549.41.
In the first month of the new business year starting April 1, the benchmark has risen nearly eight percent.
Brokers said Wall Street's rally and a gradual shift into stocks from bonds on the back of ultra-low domestic interest rates have been supportive factors.
But fund managers at major life insurers admit their purchases have contributed greatly to supporting the Nikkei average.

The next technical target for the barometer is the half-way retracement point between the June 1996 high and the January 1997 low which is seen at 19,985.22, they said. Next after that would be the 20,000 threshold.
Inflows of pension fund money, which are expected to last until June, have calmed fears over a possible meltdown in Japan's financial system.
Market sources believe the Nikkei average is establishing a floor around 19,000, nearly 1,000 points above its levels at the end of the fiscal year in March.

"The problems with financial institutions still have to be cleaned up, although the most troubled bank, Nippon Credit Bank Ltd , has started its rehabilitation," said Ken Ishikida, Sanyo Securities general manager.
"But for the time being, the market is concentrating on testing the upper side of the indices."
Despite the positive state of the market, some warn that the gains could be short-lived.

"The indices are rising without concrete buying incentives," said Kiyoshi Kimura, head of research at Societe Generale Securities. "There is a chance that the climb could stop once the allocations are spent."

Brokers said they hoped that by the time the pension funds finished their buying, higher corporate earnings, reflecting the benefit of a weakening yen against the dollar, would be announced, providing the market with pleasant surprises.

"The market has been concentrating on negative aspects such as the consumption tax rise and a slowing economy," a strategist at a second-tier brokerage said. "If the figures show that the situation is not so bad, investors could be attracted to domestic demand-related stocks."
